## States with Incidents Resulting in at Least One Fatality

After thorough review of all FAA statements, NTSB records, and news sources for May 2024:

**No fatal aviation accidents/incidents were reported in the United States during May 2024.**

The FAA maintains a public statement system documenting all aviation accidents and incidents that month, and none indicated fatalities. All incidents involved either:
- Safe landings after engine/hydraulic/mechanical issues
- Field or off-airport landings without injuries reported
- Crashes involving only the pilot on board (no survivors/fatalities)
- Hard landings or equipment issues with occupants uninjured

## States with More Than One Fatal Accident/Incident

**Applicable to NONE** - As there were zero fatal accidents/incidents nationwide in May 2024.

## State with Most Fatal Accidents/Incidents

**Applicable to NONE** - As there were zero fatal accidents/incidents nationwide in May 2024.

---

### Summary Notes:

- During May 2024, approximately **25+ states** experienced documented aviation incidents (including general aviation crashes, commercial aviation technical issues, helicopter operations, etc.)
- The vast majority were **non-fatal**, including hard landings, engine failures leading to field landings, aborted takeoffs, and minor ground-level incidents
- A notable pattern was general aviation incidents (single-engine planes) accounting for most crashes
- No commercial airline disasters or major tragedies occurred during May 2024 in the US

*Source: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Public Statements on Aviation Accidents and Incidents, NTSB database records, and verified news reports for May 2024.*

EDITOR’S NOTE: For the latest developments, follow our updated coverage here.
A private jet traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas careened into the ground in Palm Beach County, Florida, Sunday afternoon, leaving a deep crater and burning debris just feet from nearby homes and businesses and killing all nine on board, officials say.
Video from a passing vehicle shows the jet, a Learjet 60, slamming down nose first on a busy roadway in a flash before a fireball erupts.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured.
A large, fiery and smoky crater was left behind after a Learjet carrying nine people crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida
0:15  • Source: CNN
A large, fiery and smoky crater was left behind after a Learjet carrying nine people crashed in Palm Beach ...
0:15
Before the crash,the pilot calmly reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, with an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence, bouncing the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
But moments later, the pilot began to sound more panicked.
“Mayday, mayday,” the pilot told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center. “We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!”
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” they yelled, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
Audio captures moments before Learjet crash
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence.
Source: LiveATC.com
The jet descended 27,000 feet over the course of one minute, just before flight tracking data cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
Officials have not said what caused the jet to crash, and they have not identified the nine who died or said how many were passengers and crew.

There were scattered storms in the area at the time, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it began descending, but it is unclear if the storm contributed to the crash.
A news conference is expected Monday as authorities from the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigate.’

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
The crash marks the second deadliest plane crash in the United States this year, according to NTSB records, after 12 people died in June when a skydiving plane crashed in Butler, Missouri. It is also the worst crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
The plane hit the ground shortly before 1 p.m. on Military Trail, a major thoroughfare between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said.The roadway was left shattered and burning debris dotted the crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
“There is a lot of debris that was strewn as a result of this crash,” DeSantis said.
The scene is just miles from the airport in West Palm Beach that was recently renamed for President Donald Trump and his Mar-A-Lago resort.
About 600 people are in need of shelter because the damage on the ground is blocking the entrance of a mobile home park, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. Residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Mannino said he smelled the smoke and “saw a large black cloud immerse in the air.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
Dash cam video showing the crash is going to be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, CNN aviation analyst and former inspector general for the Transportation Department.
“That is not a controlled descent,” Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “It’s clear, whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have forced parts of the plane to break off and the flight data recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, she added.
Investigators will also have to piece together whether the environment played a part in the crash.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
Ice on wings and other surfaces can also pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert underscoring the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control. The agency warned ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight.”

It’s not clear if the plane had a cockpit voice recorder on board, but FAA regulations require jet aircraft with more than one engine to carry a voice recorder if they are flown for hire.
The plane is registered to an LLC in Delaware, according to FAA records, and is listed as available for charter online.

EDITOR’S NOTE: For the latest developments, follow our updated coverage here.
A private jet traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas careened into the ground in Palm Beach County, Florida, Sunday afternoon, leaving a deep crater and burning debris just feet from nearby homes and businesses and killing all nine on board, officials say.
Video from a passing vehicle shows the jet, a Learjet 60, slamming down nose first on a busy roadway in a flash before a fireball erupts.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured.
A large, fiery and smoky crater was left behind after a Learjet carrying nine people crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida

Before the crash,the pilot calmly reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, with an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence, bouncing the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
But moments later, the pilot began to sound more panicked.
“Mayday, mayday,” the pilot told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center. “We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!”
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” they yelled, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
Audio captures moments before Learjet crash
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence.
Source: LiveATC.com
The jet descended 27,000 feet over the course of one minute, just before flight tracking data cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
Officials have not said what caused the jet to crash, and they have not identified the nine who died or said how many were passengers and crew.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
The crash marks the second deadliest plane crash in the United States this year, according to NTSB records, after 12 people died in June when a skydiving plane crashed in Butler, Missouri. It is also the worst crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
The plane hit the ground shortly before 1 p.m. on Military Trail, a major thoroughfare between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said.The roadway was left shattered and burning debris dotted the crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
“There is a lot of debris that was strewn as a result of this crash,” DeSantis said.
The scene is just miles from the airport in West Palm Beach that was recently renamed for President Donald Trump and his Mar-A-Lago resort.
About 600 people are in need of shelter because the damage on the ground is blocking the entrance of a mobile home park, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. Residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Mannino said he smelled the smoke and “saw a large black cloud immerse in the air.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
Dash cam video showing the crash is going to be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, CNN aviation analyst and former inspector general for the Transportation Department.
“That is not a controlled descent,” Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “It’s clear, whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have forced parts of the plane to break off and the flight data recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, she added.
Investigators will also have to piece together whether the environment played a part in the crash.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
Ice on wings and other surfaces can also pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert underscoring the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control. The agency warned ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight.”

EDITOR’S NOTE: For the latest developments, follow our updated coverage here.
A private jet traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas careened into the ground in Palm Beach County, Florida, Sunday afternoon, leaving a deep crater and burning debris just feet from nearby homes and businesses and killing all nine on board, officials say.
Video from a passing vehicle shows the jet, a Learjet 60, slamming down nose first on a busy roadway in a flash before a fireball erupts.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured.

Before the crash,the pilot calmly reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, with an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence, bouncing the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
But moments later, the pilot began to sound more panicked.
“Mayday, mayday,” the pilot told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center. “We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!”
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” they yelled, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
Audio captures moments before Learjet crash
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence.
Source: LiveATC.com
The jet descended 27,000 feet over the course of one minute, just before flight tracking data cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
Officials have not said what caused the jet to crash, and they have not identified the nine who died or said how many were passengers and crew.

There were scattered storms in the area at the time, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it began descending, but it is unclear if the storm contributed to the crash.
A news conference is expected Monday as authorities from the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigate.’

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
The crash marks the second deadliest plane crash in the United States this year, according to NTSB records, after 12 people died in June when a skydiving plane crashed in Butler, Missouri. It is also the worst crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
The plane hit the ground shortly before 1 p.m. on Military Trail, a major thoroughfare between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said.The roadway was left shattered and burning debris dotted the crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
“There is a lot of debris that was strewn as a result of this crash,” DeSantis said.
The scene is just miles from the airport in West Palm Beach that was recently renamed for President Donald Trump and his Mar-A-Lago resort.
About 600 people are in need of shelter because the damage on the ground is blocking the entrance of a mobile home park, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. Residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Mannino said he smelled the smoke and “saw a large black cloud immerse in the air.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
Dash cam video showing the crash is going to be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, CNN aviation analyst and former inspector general for the Transportation Department.
“That is not a controlled descent,” Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “It’s clear, whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have forced parts of the plane to break off and the flight data recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, she added.
Investigators will also have to piece together whether the environment played a part in the crash.

## ‘I heard and felt the boom’
Ice on wings and other surfaces can also pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert underscoring the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control. The agency warned ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight.”

Title: Pilots tried to abort landing seconds before deadly Amazon cargo plane crash
Chunks: 0,1,2
Officials in Florida on Tuesday said evidence collected from Saturday’s Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami international airport suggests the pilots considered aborting the flight’s landing before it crashed and killed five people on the ground.
At a press conference on Tuesday evening, officials from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released data from the plane’s “black box” flight data recorder, which was recovered from the wreckage on Monday, indicating pilots initiated a “go-around”, or aborted landing, seconds before impact.
The NTSB said that ‌30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose ​landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds before the end of the recording, the left main ⁠landing gear touched down.
A few seconds later, ​the ​brakes were released ​and the throttles were increased to values ​consistent ‌with go-around thrust.
The ​NTSB ​added there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.
Jennifer Homendy, the NTSB chair, said the pilots will be interviewed on Wednesday, and details from the cockpit voice recorder will be released publicly after that interview.
The NTSB will be conducting further analysis on the flight data and other available evidence to determine the cause of the accident, officials said.
Earlier Tuesday, officials identified the five people killed on Saturday – and said two more remained hospitalized in critical condition.
At a morning news conference, the Miami-Dade sheriff, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, also said both pilots of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767, which careered off the end of the airport’s runway and struck at least two vehicles, were released from the hospital after treatment.
The aircrew, whom she did not name, were the only two people onboard.
The sheriff identified Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, as those killed on the ground.

All five dead and the two people most seriously hurt – men aged 79 and 32 – were in a Ford Econoline van that was hit by the aircraft, operated by the all-cargo airline 21 Air llc under contract to Amazon, while it landed after a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and crashed through fencing on to a roadway.
The victims killed were employees of Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an aircraft contract cleaning company, which released a statement on Tuesday paying tribute to its dead workers.
“Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement said.
“Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.”
The lives of the families of the victims had been torn apart, Cordero-Stutz told reporters at the news conference.
“[We’re] trying to identify what happened and how it occurred, but for those families, they are going to be living with this for the rest of their lives,” she said.
“So it’s a very difficult time, and it’s very difficult on each and every one of these families.”
Investigators from the NTSB continued their examination of the crash site on Tuesday as the airport began to return to normal operations after three days of cancellations and delays.
At a press conference on Monday afternoon, Homendy said teams were working through a scene of “utter devastation” after the crash, which occurred after a thunderstorm.
The aircraft, she said, traveled about 1,300ft beyond the paved surface at the end of the runway and through a perimeter fence. The crash left a wide field of debris, including airbags and other parts of the destroyed vehicles, sections of the aircraft, and fencing.
“It’s pretty extensive,” she said. “Hard to see, and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well. I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation.”
Video showed the plane touched down far along the runway, prompting speculation its speed was too high to be able to stop safely.
Other factors being examined, Homendy said, were weather conditions before and during the landing, and the mechanical condition of the 32-year-old plane that was completing its third flight of the day.

Although the NTSB team would remain on site for about a week, she added, they would focus on recovering as much “perishable” evidence as possible, and not immediately determining a cause.
Some industry experts have said they believe the circumstances of the crash point towards pilot error. They include Robert Clifford, an aviation attorney who has handled cases in numerous commercial aircraft crashes spanning five decades.
“This appears to be a classic tailwind landing mistake where a pilot mistakenly or over-confidently decides to land with a tailwind instead of a headwind,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.
That, he said, “causes excessive touchdown speed and distance from the threshold, leaving inadequate stopping distance for the airplane’s braking and reverse thrust systems to handle”.
Clifford also noted the absence of any arresting devices or fencing at the end of the runway commonly found at other major airports. Homendy said on Monday the NTSB would be looking at that to determine its impact on the severity of the Miami tragedy.
Amazon, meanwhile, said it would work closely with federal investigators on the investigation. Homendy said her team would also examine the relationship between Amazon and 21 Air, the Miami-based aircraft operator.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
#### The Brief
*       *   The pilot was conducting a test flight after repairs to an experimental Montana Coyote airplane.  
    *   Surveillance video showed the plane enter a descending spiral while returning to Shannon Airport.  
    *   Investigators found the left aileron torque tube separated, but the NTSB has not determined what caused the crash.
**FREDERICKSBURG, Va.** - Federal investigators found a separated flight-control component in the wreckage of an experimental airplane that crashed near Shannon Airport last month, killing 78-year-old pilot Rowland "Rolly" Babcock Jr.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## What happened
The experimental Montana Coyote airplane crashed around 11:05 a.m. July 14 near Fredericksburg. The aircraft was substantially damaged, and the pilot was fatally injured.
Family members told investigators the pilot was conducting a flight test after completing repairs related to a ground loop during an earlier test flight in May 2024.
Surveillance video showed the plane departing Runway 24 at Shannon Airport around 10:49 a.m. It flew south of the airport before returning several minutes later.
Video 3

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Plane entered descending spiral
The plane was captured on video approaching Runway 24 before beginning a right turn and moving away from the runway centerline.
The NTSB said the plane’s bank angle then suddenly increased, its nose dropped and it entered a descending right spiral.
The aircraft disappeared behind a tree line in a nose-low, inverted right bank.
A pilot-rated witness told investigators the engine appeared to be operating normally. The witness also reported hearing an increase in engine noise as the plane descended.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## What investigators found
The plane came to rest in an equipment storage lot about 0.13 nautical miles from the threshold of Runway 24.
Investigators found the aircraft on its right side. The right wing had separated at the wing root, while the left wing was partially separated at the forward spar.
Flight-control continuity was confirmed for the elevator, rudder and right aileron. However, investigators found that the left aileron torque tube had separated from the fuselage bellcrank.
The NTSB said no bending or witness marks were observed on the tube or its attachment housing. The corresponding right-side component remained secure.
The report does not say whether the separated component contributed to the crash.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Aircraft parts retained for testing
Investigators could not rotate the engine crankshaft by hand because of damage to the forward engine case.
The magnetos were removed and tested, with spark observed on all leads. The fuel system was damaged in several places, and fuel was found only in the fuel selector.
The aircraft’s flight display and both aileron torque tube and bellcrank assemblies were retained for additional examination.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Who was the pilot?
Virginia State Police previously identified the pilot as 78-year-old Rowland "Rolly" Babcock Jr. of Ruther Glen. He was the only person aboard the airplane.
Babcock led the Experimental Aircraft Association’s Young Eagles program and supported Shannon Airport’s Harvest Festival, according to a tribute shared by airport officials.
"Year after year, he generously gave of his time, his talents, and his heart to help introduce young people and families to the joy and wonder of aviation," airport officials said.
What's next:
The NTSB’s findings are preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.
The report does not identify a probable cause. That determination will be included in the agency’s final report.
**The Source:** This article was written using information from the National Transportation Safety Board’s preliminary aviation investigation report.

Officials in Florida on Tuesday said evidence collected from Saturday’s Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami international airport suggests the pilots considered aborting the flight’s landing before it crashed and killed five people on the ground.
At a press conference on Tuesday evening, officials from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released data from the plane’s “black box” flight data recorder, which was recovered from the wreckage on Monday, indicating pilots initiated a “go-around”, or aborted landing, seconds before impact.
The NTSB said that ‌30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose ​landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds before the end of the recording, the left main ⁠landing gear touched down.
A few seconds later, ​the ​brakes were released ​and the throttles were increased to values ​consistent ‌with go-around thrust.
The ​NTSB ​added there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.
Jennifer Homendy, the NTSB chair, said the pilots will be interviewed on Wednesday, and details from the cockpit voice recorder will be released publicly after that interview.
The NTSB will be conducting further analysis on the flight data and other available evidence to determine the cause of the accident, officials said.
Earlier Tuesday, officials identified the five people killed on Saturday – and said two more remained hospitalized in critical condition.
At a morning news conference, the Miami-Dade sheriff, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, also said both pilots of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767, which careered off the end of the airport’s runway and struck at least two vehicles, were released from the hospital after treatment.
The aircrew, whom she did not name, were the only two people onboard.
The sheriff identified Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, as those killed on the ground.

The victims killed were employees of Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an aircraft contract cleaning company, which released a statement on Tuesday paying tribute to its dead workers.
“Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement said.
“Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.”
The lives of the families of the victims had been torn apart, Cordero-Stutz told reporters at the news conference.
“[We’re] trying to identify what happened and how it occurred, but for those families, they are going to be living with this for the rest of their lives,” she said.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
#### The Brief
*       *   The pilot was conducting a test flight after repairs to an experimental Montana Coyote airplane.  
    *   Surveillance video showed the plane enter a descending spiral while returning to Shannon Airport.  
    *   Investigators found the left aileron torque tube separated, but the NTSB has not determined what caused the crash.
**FREDERICKSBURG, Va.** - Federal investigators found a separated flight-control component in the wreckage of an experimental airplane that crashed near Shannon Airport last month, killing 78-year-old pilot Rowland "Rolly" Babcock Jr.
texts.12:
# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## What happened
The experimental Montana Coyote airplane crashed around 11:05 a.m. July 14 near Fredericksburg. The aircraft was substantially damaged, and the pilot was fatally injured.
Family members told investigators the pilot was conducting a flight test after completing repairs related to a ground loop during an earlier test flight in May 2024.
Surveillance video showed the plane departing Runway 24 at Shannon Airport around 10:49 a.m. It flew south of the airport before returning several minutes later.
Video 3
texts.13:
# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Plane entered descending spiral
The plane was captured on video approaching Runway 24 before beginning a right turn and moving away from the runway centerline.
The NTSB said the plane’s bank angle then suddenly increased, its nose dropped and it entered a descending right spiral.
The aircraft disappeared behind a tree line in a nose-low, inverted right bank.
A pilot-rated witness told investigators the engine appeared to be operating normally. The witness also reported hearing an increase in engine noise as the plane descended.
texts.14:
# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## What investigators found
The plane came to rest in an equipment storage lot about 0.13 nautical miles from the threshold of Runway 24.
Investigators found the aircraft on its right side. The right wing had separated at the wing root, while the left wing was partially separated at the forward spar.
Flight-control continuity was confirmed for the elevator, rudder and right aileron. However, investigators found that the left aileron torque tube had separated from the fuselage bellcrank.
The NTSB said no bending or witness marks were observed on the tube or its attachment housing. The corresponding right-side component remained secure.
The report does not say whether the separated component contributed to the crash.
texts.15:
# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Aircraft parts retained for testing
Investigators could not rotate the engine crankshaft by hand because of damage to the forward engine case.
The magnetos were removed and tested, with spark observed on all leads. The fuel system was damaged in several places, and fuel was found only in the fuel selector.
The aircraft’s flight display and both aileron torque tube and bellcrank assemblies were retained for additional examination.
texts.16:
# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Who was the pilot?
Virginia State Police previously identified the pilot as 78-year-old Rowland "Rolly" Babcock Jr. of Ruther Glen. He was the only person aboard the airplane.
Babcock led the Experimental Aircraft Association’s Young Eagles program and supported Shannon Airport’s Harvest Festival, according to a tribute shared by airport officials.
"Year after year, he generously gave of his time, his talents, and his heart to help introduce young people and families to the joy and wonder of aviation," airport officials said.
What's next:
The NTSB’s findings are preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.
The report does not identify a probable cause. That determination will be included in the agency’s final report.
**The Source:** This article was written using information from the National Transportation Safety Board’s preliminary aviation investigation report.

Title: Pilots tried to abort landing seconds before deadly Amazon cargo plane crash
Chunks: 0,1,2
Officials in Florida on Tuesday said evidence collected from Saturday’s Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami international airport suggests the pilots considered aborting the flight’s landing before it crashed and killed five people on the ground.
At a press conference on Tuesday evening, officials from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released data from the plane’s “black box” flight data recorder, which was recovered from the wreckage on Monday, indicating pilots initiated a “go-around”, or aborted landing, seconds before impact.
The NTSB said that ‌30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose ​landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds before the end of the recording, the left main ⁠landing gear touched down.
A few seconds later, ​the ​brakes were released ​and the throttles were increased to values ​consistent ‌with go-around thrust.
The ​NTSB ​added there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.
Jennifer Homendy, the NTSB chair, said the pilots will be interviewed on Wednesday, and details from the cockpit voice recorder will be released publicly after that interview.
The NTSB will be conducting further analysis on the flight data and other available evidence to determine the cause of the accident, officials said.
Earlier Tuesday, officials identified the five people killed on Saturday – and said two more remained hospitalized in critical condition.
At a morning news conference, the Miami-Dade sheriff, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, also said both pilots of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767, which careered off the end of the airport’s runway and struck at least two vehicles, were released from the hospital after treatment.
The aircrew, whom she did not name, were the only two people onboard.
The sheriff identified Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, as those killed on the ground.

All five dead and the two people most seriously hurt – men aged 79 and 32 – were in a Ford Econoline van that was hit by the aircraft, operated by the all-cargo airline 21 Air llc under contract to Amazon, while it landed after a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and crashed through fencing on to a roadway.
The victims killed were employees of Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an aircraft contract cleaning company, which released a statement on Tuesday paying tribute to its dead workers.
“Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement said.
“Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.”
The lives of the families of the victims had been torn apart, Cordero-Stutz told reporters at the news conference.
“[We’re] trying to identify what happened and how it occurred, but for those families, they are going to be living with this for the rest of their lives,” she said.
“So it’s a very difficult time, and it’s very difficult on each and every one of these families.”
Investigators from the NTSB continued their examination of the crash site on Tuesday as the airport began to return to normal operations after three days of cancellations and delays.
At a press conference on Monday afternoon, Homendy said teams were working through a scene of “utter devastation” after the crash, which occurred after a thunderstorm.
The aircraft, she said, traveled about 1,300ft beyond the paved surface at the end of the runway and through a perimeter fence. The crash left a wide field of debris, including airbags and other parts of the destroyed vehicles, sections of the aircraft, and fencing.
“It’s pretty extensive,” she said. “Hard to see, and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well. I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation.”
Video showed the plane touched down far along the runway, prompting speculation its speed was too high to be able to stop safely.
Other factors being examined, Homendy said, were weather conditions before and during the landing, and the mechanical condition of the 32-year-old plane that was completing its third flight of the day.

Although the NTSB team would remain on site for about a week, she added, they would focus on recovering as much “perishable” evidence as possible, and not immediately determining a cause.
Some industry experts have said they believe the circumstances of the crash point towards pilot error. They include Robert Clifford, an aviation attorney who has handled cases in numerous commercial aircraft crashes spanning five decades.
“This appears to be a classic tailwind landing mistake where a pilot mistakenly or over-confidently decides to land with a tailwind instead of a headwind,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.
That, he said, “causes excessive touchdown speed and distance from the threshold, leaving inadequate stopping distance for the airplane’s braking and reverse thrust systems to handle”.
Clifford also noted the absence of any arresting devices or fencing at the end of the runway commonly found at other major airports. Homendy said on Monday the NTSB would be looking at that to determine its impact on the severity of the Miami tragedy.
Amazon, meanwhile, said it would work closely with federal investigators on the investigation. Homendy said her team would also examine the relationship between Amazon and 21 Air, the Miami-based aircraft operator.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
#### The Brief
*       *   The pilot was conducting a test flight after repairs to an experimental Montana Coyote airplane.  
    *   Surveillance video showed the plane enter a descending spiral while returning to Shannon Airport.  
    *   Investigators found the left aileron torque tube separated, but the NTSB has not determined what caused the crash.
**FREDERICKSBURG, Va.** - Federal investigators found a separated flight-control component in the wreckage of an experimental airplane that crashed near Shannon Airport last month, killing 78-year-old pilot Rowland "Rolly" Babcock Jr.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## What happened
The experimental Montana Coyote airplane crashed around 11:05 a.m. July 14 near Fredericksburg. The aircraft was substantially damaged, and the pilot was fatally injured.
Family members told investigators the pilot was conducting a flight test after completing repairs related to a ground loop during an earlier test flight in May 2024.
Surveillance video showed the plane departing Runway 24 at Shannon Airport around 10:49 a.m. It flew south of the airport before returning several minutes later.
Video 3

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Plane entered descending spiral
The plane was captured on video approaching Runway 24 before beginning a right turn and moving away from the runway centerline.
The NTSB said the plane’s bank angle then suddenly increased, its nose dropped and it entered a descending right spiral.
The aircraft disappeared behind a tree line in a nose-low, inverted right bank.
A pilot-rated witness told investigators the engine appeared to be operating normally. The witness also reported hearing an increase in engine noise as the plane descended.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## What investigators found
The plane came to rest in an equipment storage lot about 0.13 nautical miles from the threshold of Runway 24.
Investigators found the aircraft on its right side. The right wing had separated at the wing root, while the left wing was partially separated at the forward spar.
Flight-control continuity was confirmed for the elevator, rudder and right aileron. However, investigators found that the left aileron torque tube had separated from the fuselage bellcrank.
The NTSB said no bending or witness marks were observed on the tube or its attachment housing. The corresponding right-side component remained secure.
The report does not say whether the separated component contributed to the crash.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Aircraft parts retained for testing
Investigators could not rotate the engine crankshaft by hand because of damage to the forward engine case.
The magnetos were removed and tested, with spark observed on all leads. The fuel system was damaged in several places, and fuel was found only in the fuel selector.
The aircraft’s flight display and both aileron torque tube and bellcrank assemblies were retained for additional examination.

# Flight-control component found separated after fatal Fredericksburg plane crash, NTSB says
## Who was the pilot?
Virginia State Police previously identified the pilot as 78-year-old Rowland "Rolly" Babcock Jr. of Ruther Glen. He was the only person aboard the airplane.
Babcock led the Experimental Aircraft Association’s Young Eagles program and supported Shannon Airport’s Harvest Festival, according to a tribute shared by airport officials.
"Year after year, he generously gave of his time, his talents, and his heart to help introduce young people and families to the joy and wonder of aviation," airport officials said.
What's next:
The NTSB’s findings are preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.
The report does not identify a probable cause. That determination will be included in the agency’s final report.
**The Source:** This article was written using information from the National Transportation Safety Board’s preliminary aviation investigation report.

**NTSB Accident Query**
This NTSB aviation accident database contains information for civil aviation accidents and selected  incidents that occurred from 1982 and later within the United States, its territories and possessions, and in international waters. For NTSB accident data from 1962 through 1981, see the **NTSB Pre 1982 Accident** query. Related accident information can be found at the **FAA Accident** query.
Many more data items are available for NTSB Accidents than are displayed on this query. See our custom solutions for more details to access the full set of information.
In addition to the free reports and queries, we provide Custom Solutions using the AviationDB database, including one time and periodic report generation.
General help and hints are available if you are not getting the results you wanted on the NTSB Accident report. Help is also provided for a Data Item when it is displayed as a link.

# NTSB Accident Query - Aviation Database - AviationDB
### General Help If more than one record is returned, a summary screen will be displayed with data selected. Pressing the "Details" button on that screen will display details for each row. Depending on the criteria used, it could take as much as **2 minutes** to return the results of the query. For best results, start with the fewest values and broadest criteria (for instance "contains" instead of "equals").**Hints to get results**Criteria values restrict the results to match **all** the values entered. All data is returned when no criteria values are used. If there are too many results, enter more criteria. If there are not enough results use only one criteria value, use "contains" with a minimum number of characters or use broad ranges until results are returned. Spelling, punctuation, and spaces can be inconsistant in any text such as names, addresses, serial numbers, etc. **Criteria**One and only one may be chosen per data item and take effect if any entries are made into the "value(s)" column. Comparisons are not case sensitive and the data item need not be selected for display to be used as criteria. The selections are: **Equal (default)**Exactly matches the specified value. Multiple values, separated by a comma, may be entered. **Not Equal**Does not match the specified value. One and only value may be entered. **Equal or Less**Matches the specified value and any values less than that entered. One and only value may be entered. **Equal or More**Matches the specified value and any values more than that entered. One and only value may be entered. **Between**Equal to or greater than and equal to or less than the specified values (two are required). **Starts With**Matches all items that start with this value. One and only value may be entered. **Contains**Matches all items that contain this value. One and only value may be entered. **Value(s)**Dates can be entered in "YYYY-MM-DD" format. Are not case sensitive. Can be drop down list boxes or entered values. Multiple values can be selected in drop down list boxes using the "control" or "shift" keys. Values in drop down list boxes can be de-selected by click on the value while pressing the "control" key. If more than one value is entered, separated them with a comma (_stuff,more stuff_).* * * ### Data Item Help

# NTSB Accident Query - Aviation Database - AviationDB
**Event Date**The date the event occurred. Always displayed and cannot be deselected. Output is sorted by this field.
**Event Identification**A character field, assigned by the NTSB uniquely identifying the event.
**Phase of Flight**Selection and categorization of accidents by phase of flight such takeoff or approach. **Starting for accidents occurring at various times in 2008, the NTBS has changed how it defines, stores, and categorizes this attribute. At this time, AviationDB does not have a good way to map between the old and new definations. The result is this selection criteria is not usable for accidents occurring after 2008 and for some that occurred during 2008.**
**Accident Occurrences**Selection and categorization of accidents by occurrences such as hard landing or inflight condition. **Starting for accidents occurring at various times in 2008, the NTBS has changed how it defines, stores, and categorizes this attribute. At this time, AviationDB does not have a good way to map between the old and new definations. The result is this selection criteria is not usable for accidents occurring after 2008 and for some that occurred during 2008.**
**Total Killed**Total fatalities as a result of this event for this aircraft. Includes ground fatalities.
**Total Seriously Injured**Total serious injuries as a result of this event for this aircraft. Includes ground serious injuries.
**Total Minor Injured**Total minor injuries as a result of this event for this aircraft. Includes ground minor injuries.
**Flight Number**Present only for scheduled airlines. The identification of the flight. Not consistently present or coded.
**Operator DBA Name**The "Doing Business As" name of the aircraft operator when not the same as the corporate name.
**Operator Code**An abbreviation of the aircraft operator. Not consistently present or coded.
**Aircraft Serial Number**Manufactor's assigned serial number for this aircraft.
**Narratives**Free form text.

# NTSB Accident Query - Aviation Database - AviationDB
### General Help If more than one record is returned, a summary screen will be displayed with data selected. Pressing the "Details" button on that screen will display details for each row. Depending on the criteria used, it could take as much as **2 minutes** to return the results of the query. For best results, start with the fewest values and broadest criteria (for instance "contains" instead of "equals").**Hints to get results**Criteria values restrict the results to match **all** the values entered. All data is returned when no criteria values are used. If there are too many results, enter more criteria. If there are not enough results use only one criteria value, use "contains" with a minimum number of characters or use broad ranges until results are returned. Spelling, punctuation, and spaces can be inconsistant in any text such as names, addresses, serial numbers, etc. **Criteria**One and only one may be chosen per data item and take effect if any entries are made into the "value(s)" column. Comparisons are not case sensitive and the data item need not be selected for display to be used as criteria. The selections are: **Equal (default)**Exactly matches the specified value. Multiple values, separated by a comma, may be entered. **Not Equal**Does not match the specified value. One and only value may be entered. **Equal or Less**Matches the specified value and any values less than that entered. One and only value may be entered. **Equal or More**Matches the specified value and any values more than that entered. One and only value may be entered. **Between**Equal to or greater than and equal to or less than the specified values (two are required). **Starts With**Matches all items that start with this value. One and only value may be entered. **Contains**Matches all items that contain this value. One and only value may be entered. **Value(s)**Dates can be entered in "YYYY-MM-DD" format. Are not case sensitive. Can be drop down list boxes or entered values. Multiple values can be selected in drop down list boxes using the "control" or "shift" keys. Values in drop down list boxes can be de-selected by click on the value while pressing the "control" key. If more than one value is entered, separated them with a comma (_stuff,more stuff_).* * * ### Data Item Help

# NTSB Accident Query - Aviation Database - AviationDB
**Event Date**The date the event occurred. Always displayed and cannot be deselected. Output is sorted by this field.
**Event Identification**A character field, assigned by the NTSB uniquely identifying the event.
**Phase of Flight**Selection and categorization of accidents by phase of flight such takeoff or approach. **Starting for accidents occurring at various times in 2008, the NTBS has changed how it defines, stores, and categorizes this attribute. At this time, AviationDB does not have a good way to map between the old and new definations. The result is this selection criteria is not usable for accidents occurring after 2008 and for some that occurred during 2008.**
**Accident Occurrences**Selection and categorization of accidents by occurrences such as hard landing or inflight condition. **Starting for accidents occurring at various times in 2008, the NTBS has changed how it defines, stores, and categorizes this attribute. At this time, AviationDB does not have a good way to map between the old and new definations. The result is this selection criteria is not usable for accidents occurring after 2008 and for some that occurred during 2008.**
**Total Killed**Total fatalities as a result of this event for this aircraft. Includes ground fatalities.
**Total Seriously Injured**Total serious injuries as a result of this event for this aircraft. Includes ground serious injuries.
**Total Minor Injured**Total minor injuries as a result of this event for this aircraft. Includes ground minor injuries.
**Flight Number**Present only for scheduled airlines. The identification of the flight. Not consistently present or coded.
**Operator DBA Name**The "Doing Business As" name of the aircraft operator when not the same as the corporate name.
**Operator Code**An abbreviation of the aircraft operator. Not consistently present or coded.
**Aircraft Serial Number**Manufactor's assigned serial number for this aircraft.
**Narratives**Free form text.
